    data = df

    , random = .(subject,batch)
    , fixed = .(exposure,asthma,atopy,gender)
)

messages.subject_clean: How to compute simple effects
messages.body_plain:
Here is an old blog entry of mine on how to do this from generic
software output (including potentially R).

http://psychologicalstatistics.blogspot.com/2006/07/how-to-calculate-simple-main-effects.html

However, I would caution about using simple main effects to follow-up
an interaction (and I have somewhat changed my view of their utility
since I wrote that entry). They aren't really interaction follow-ups.
The simple main effects decompose Sums of Squares attributed to the
interaction and to one of the main effects. So if you have a
hypothesis about an interaction, simple main effects may simply be a
way of testing that hypothesis that decreases power (e.g., by reducing
n or carving the interaction in 'smaller' effects that are harder to
detect). If the interaction has 1 treatment df (e.g., 2 x 2 ANOVA)
then it is a focused test that can't be decomposed further. If the
interaction has multiple treatment df then it can be decomposed
further - but the correct method is an interaction contrast (not
simple main effects).

Simple main effects may be useful if they reflect the hypothesis of
interest.

Thom

messages.body_plain:
You'll have to re-organize your data into what is called "long" data
format. This can be achieved by:

install.packages('reshape2') #not necessary if it's already installed
library(reshape2)
my_long_data = melt.data.frame(
    data = my_data
    , id.vars = c('Specie','Mother','Treatment','Rep')
    , variable_name = 'Dias'
)

Then you can perform your ANOVA. However, I suspect that ANOVA is not
the right tool for you. Count data is unlikely to be Gaussian
distributed, so you'll want a statistical tool that can provide a link
to a more appropriate error distribution, like the poisson
distribution. Also, I suspect that your design would benefit from
being able to specify multiple random effects (from what you describe,
it sounds like gerbox and mother are crossed random effects). So, I'd
look into mixed effects modelling if I were you. Here are a couple
good resource pages:

http://lme4.r-forge.r-project.org

http://glmm.wikidot.com

http://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/tagged/mixed-model

messages.subject: Re: How to compute simple effects
messages.subject_clean: How to compute simple effects
messages.body_plain:
It depends on design. The simple main effects for within subjects/
repeated
measures factors are just one-way ANOVAs on the subset of the data you
are
interested in. For between subject factors just get the MSe from the
original
ANOVA and then you can compute in R from a vector of cell means in a
balanced design. so something like this should work:

ms.error <- 10
cell.means <- c(14, 16, 22, 23)
n <- 10

ss.sme <- n * var(cell.means)
df.sme <- length(cell.means) - 1
ms.sme <- ss.sme / df.sme
F.sme <- ms.sme / ms.error
F.sme
pf(F.sme, df.sme, df.error, lower.tail=FALSE)

For a between-subject factor in a mixed design you need to pool two
error terms and it is fiddly, though there is an excel spreadsheet on
my
blog that does this. For some reason I never implemented this in R
but it is a simple matter of pooling the variances and using a
Welch-Satterthwaite style correction for the df.

For contrasts, you can run them fairly easily in the gmodels or
multcomp
packages. The gmodels packages is more versatile (e.g., working with
mer and lme objects) while multcomp has options for multiple
comparison
prodecures that are more powerful than those in SPSS or Statistica. In
fact,
SPSS contrasts are extremely hard to set up for anything other than
contrasts on a single factor.

Thom

On Thu, Oct 27, 2011 at 10:41 PM, Matthew Malter Cohen
<matthewma...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I am having a little trouble understanding L10LRa & L10LRb. From your
> documentation, these are log10 likelihood ratio of AIC and BIC
> respectively. Does this mean that when one receives a negative value
> (-2), the model including that variable is unlikely (1 to 100)? And
> values like 2, indicate a likelihood of 100 to 1?

Yes, with the amendment that, because the values represent the ratio
of two likelihoods, the interpretation is relative; -2 means that the
unrestricted model is rather unlikely relative to the restricted
model, while +2 means that the unrestricted model is rather likely
relative to the restricted model.

In more recent versions of ez (https://github.com/mike-lawrence/ez) I
have transitioned from log-base-10 scale to log-base-2 scale, where
it's possible to talk about the values as representing "bits of
evidence" for or against the effect (relative to its respective null).
(I also report the AIC correction only, as further investigation
revealed that BIC assumes that the True model is amongst the models
being compared, which I'd say is rarely the case in science). You also
might find the dev version of ezMixed useful because it uses GAMM for
evaluating possibly-non-linear continuous variables, as Age might be
in your data.
